long_synopsis: Week 32 turned Washington, D.C. into a laboratory for expanded federal power: a declared crime emergency, armed National Guard troops, a Union Station takeover, and threats of similar deployments to Chicago and Baltimore. Alongside this, prosecutors investigated administration critics, a flag-burning prosecution order tested First Amendment limits, and Trump moved to eliminate mail-in voting nationally while redistricting fights intensified in Utah, Texas, and California. The CDC director was fired and officials resigned in protest; FEMA whistleblowers faced retaliation. Labor protections for federal workers, contractors, and care workers were rolled back within days. Courts still imposed real limits, blocking sanctuary defunding, dismissing a suit against Maryland's judges, and halting one deportation. The clock moved only slightly, from 7:41 to 7:42 p.m., but the week's breadth mattered more than any single event.
short_synopsis: Washington became a proving ground for federalized policing and emergency powers, while prosecutorial pressure, agency purges, labor rollbacks, and voting restrictions spread the same logic outward. Courts offered a thin but real counterweight. The clock advanced only slightly, reflecting confirmation more than rupture.
